content.text:
🤖

tmux is a terminal multiplexer: a small program that sits between you and one or more shells so those sessions outlive a dropped SSH connection, a closed laptop lid, or a crashed GUI terminal. You attach to a tmux **server**, which owns **sessions**. Each session holds **windows** (like tabs), and each window can be split into **panes**. Detaching does not stop work. Reattaching from another machine, days later, restores the same layout, running processes, and scrollback.

That persistence is why people still reach for tmux on remote servers. A long compile, a training job, or a database migration can keep running after the network dies. On a laptop it is equally useful: you can leave a development stack—editor, logs, tests—arranged once and return to it without rebuilding the layout. Pairing and teaching also benefit: two people can attach to the same session and see the same terminals, with optional read-only attaches for observers.

The mental model is a tree. The server is a daemon, usually started on first `tmux` invocation. A session is a named workspace (`work`, `prod`, `notes`). Windows are numbered and optionally named; they share the session but not the visible screen unless you use a shared window. Panes divide a window into a grid. Focus moves with keyboard prefixes. The default prefix is `Ctrl-b`, then a second key: `c` creates a window, `%` and `"` split vertically and horizontally, `d` detaches, `[` enters copy mode. Almost every binding can be remapped in `~/.tmux.conf`.

Copy mode is easy to underestimate. It lets you scroll history with vi or emacs keys, search, and yank text into tmux’s paste buffer, then into the system clipboard with a plugin or `pbcopy`/`xclip` hook. For people who live in SSH, this is often faster than fighting terminal selection across nested sessions. Nested tmux (local tmux wrapping remote tmux) is common and slightly awkward: you send the inner prefix by pressing the outer prefix twice, or you change one of the prefixes so they do not collide.

Configuration is a plain text file of `set` and `bind` commands. Status bars can show session name, window list, hostname, load, git branch, or battery. Plugins, notably via TPM (Tmux Plugin Manager), add themes, sensible defaults, resurrect/continuum (save and restore sessions across reboots), and clipboard integration. Resurrect is not magic: it snapshots layout and some process names; it cannot always revive a REPL’s in-memory state. Treat it as a layout saver, not a full VM snapshot.

tmux competes with GNU screen, terminal tabs, iTerm2 splits, Zellij, and IDE integrated terminals. Screen is older and still present on locked-down hosts; tmux’s window/pane model and scripting are generally nicer. Desktop terminal splits die with the window. Zellij offers a more modern UI and discoverable keybindings; tmux wins on ubiquity, muscle memory, and being already installed on many servers. Choose based on where you work, not fashion.

Scripting is a quiet superpower. `tmux new-session -d -s build` starts work in the background. `send-keys` types into a pane. `split-window` and `select-layout` assemble a dashboard: logs left, REPL right, tests below. Teams check a `dev.tmux` script into a repo so every engineer gets the same panes. Combined with SSH config (`RemoteCommand tmux attach -t main || tmux new -s main`), login can drop you into a durable workspace automatically.

Pain points exist. The prefix tax annoys newcomers. Mouse support is optional and can fight with terminal selection. Version differences between macOS’s old tmux, Linux packages, and source builds break configs that use newer options. True color and italic fonts need terminal and tmux settings to agree (`terminal-overrides`, `default-terminal`). Inside Docker or restricted environments, a missing `tmux` binary is a reminder that the multiplexer is a host tool, not something the container always provides.

A practical starter kit is small: rename sessions, name windows, split two or three panes, detach without fear, and learn copy mode. Add a status line you can read at a glance. Bind `r` to reload the config. Disable the delay after Escape if you use vim (`escape-time`). Turn on mouse if you want it, then learn the keys anyway for remote machines without a mouse. When a job must not die, start it in tmux first, not after you realize you forgot `nohup`.

tmux is not an editor, an IDE, or a window manager for the whole desktop. It is a durable, scriptable layer for interactive shells. Used that way, it removes a whole class of “I lost my SSH session and my work” accidents, and it turns a blank terminal into a workspace you can leave and return to. Six hundred words is enough to say the rest is practice: attach, split, detach, attach again, until it feels like the terminal you always meant to have.
